speaker: Bryan Cantrill
title: The history of servers, the cloud, and what’s next – with Oxide
question: In infrastructure software, why is live-updating a full-stack distributed system fundamentally harder than updating a standalone application?
guest: The whole thing needs to be updated—you have to be able to update all of the software in the rack. This is not just updating the operating system; it's updating the service processor, the root of trust, the drive firmware, the host operating system, and all of the distributed components that speak to one another. And that challenge is fractally complicated. At a very basic level, when you're updating, you are moving the system from one version to another, and in between, it's in both versions. What does it mean to keep the system operable while you have some new components and some old components? What if you change your database schema from one version to the next? You have to reason about the system in that hybrid state, make every component independently updatable, and build a robust foundation first—then slowly automate different aspects over time while treating quality as the hard constraint.

points.core: Rack-scale updates must span every layer from low-level firmware to control-plane services.
points.note: Accept: updating heterogeneous layers together—service processor, root of trust, drive firmware, host OS, and distributed control plane—not just one binary. Do not credit: generic statements that servers have 'more code' or 'more dependencies.'

points.core: Rolling updates temporarily place the cluster into a mixed-version hybrid state.
points.note: Accept: nodes/components running both old and new versions simultaneously during an online upgrade instead of an atomic swap. Do not credit: assuming downtime or offline full-cluster replacement solves the core problem.

points.core: Communicating components must remain interoperable across mixed versions throughout the transition.
points.note: Accept: backward/forward protocol compatibility across interacting services while nodes upgrade asynchronously. Do not credit: generic advice to 'test thoroughly' or 'use CI/CD' without mixed-version interoperability.

points.core: Database schema migrations must keep the system operable across coexisting versions.
points.note: Accept: online/expand-contract schema evolution so both old and new code can read and write state safely during rollout. Do not credit: vague mentions of 'database backups' or 'rolling back' without version-coexistence schema handling.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A standalone application can be updated atomically: you stop one process, swap the binary, and restart, so there is only ever one version running against its own state. A full-stack distributed system can't do that, for several compounding reasons.

The update is never instantaneous across nodes, so old and new versions must coexist and interoperate mid-rollout. That means every wire protocol, RPC interface, and on-disk or replicated data format has to be backward and forward compatible, often across multiple versions, and rollback must remain possible even after new-format data has been written.

The system must also keep serving while it changes. Nodes hold in-flight requests, replicated state, leases, and quorum membership, so taking them down has to be coordinated to preserve availability and consistency, and a restart looks just like a failure to the rest of the cluster.

Finally, the layers depend on each other: kernel, hypervisor, storage, networking, control plane, and services each have their own upgrade ordering constraints, and the orchestration machinery performing the update is itself part of what is being updated. Partial failures mid-upgrade leave the system in mixed states that are combinatorially hard to test.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Updating a standalone application happens within a single machine and failure domain, allowing an atomic process cutover or localized state handoff. By contrast, live-updating a full-stack distributed infrastructure system cannot halt the cluster or upgrade every node simultaneously without breaking availability guarantees for the live workloads—such as virtual machines, storage volumes, and active network flows—running atop it.

Consequently, rolling updates force old and new software versions to coexist and interact in production. Every wire protocol, RPC interface, consensus message, and persistent data schema must maintain backward and forward compatibility across multi-phase rollouts, because upgraded nodes may emit requests or mutate shared state that un-upgraded peers must still understand—especially if an error forces a rollback before irreversible state migrations complete. Full-stack coupling compounds the difficulty: changes span interdependent kernel, data-plane, control-plane, and storage layers, requiring live state transfer or workload draining across vertical and horizontal boundaries while preserving quorum safety, consistency invariants, and tail-latency SLAs amid routine hardware failures and network partitions occurring mid-upgrade.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Updating a standalone application means swapping one binary at one moment, with one owner of its state. A full-stack distributed system can't be updated atomically. It has to be rolled out piece by piece while it keeps serving traffic, so for some window old and new versions of nodes, services, schemas and protocols run side by side and must interoperate. Every change therefore needs backward and forward compatibility in wire formats, APIs, on-disk data and replicated state. In practice that means multi-phase migrations such as expand, migrate, then contract, rather than one cutover.

The layers also depend on each other. The kernel, runtime, orchestration, storage, networking and application layers each have their own version constraints, and the order of upgrades matters. State is spread across replicas and caches, so a migration has to preserve consensus, quorum and data invariants while nodes restart. Partial failures, network partitions and timing differences mean an upgrade can stall halfway, which leaves mixed-version states that are hard to test exhaustively. Rolling back is often unsafe once new-format data has been written.

So the hard part isn't installing code. It's keeping a running, stateful system correct across every intermediate state of the transition.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Updating a standalone application is essentially atomic: you can pause it, replace its binary and local state, and restart it so only one version ever runs at a time. Live-updating a full-stack distributed system eliminates that simplicity because the system must stay available while nodes and layers—from kernels and networking to storage engines and control planes—upgrade asynchronously. During a rollout, old and new versions run simultaneously and continuously interact over unreliable networks. Every wire protocol, RPC schema, and on-disk data format must therefore maintain strict forward and backward compatibility, preventing any single change from breaking in-flight requests or distributed consensus. Cross-layer dependencies compound this risk, since a benign change in one tier can trigger subtle timing bugs, resource contention, or cascading failures in another only under live production traffic. Finally, rollbacks are rarely clean: once newer nodes write updated state or alter shared schemas, reverting can corrupt data or split the cluster unless every migration is carefully staged in reversible phases.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A standalone application often has one process and one local state boundary. An updater can pause it, replace the code, migrate its state, and restart it. A live distributed system has to keep serving requests while independently running components change at different times. During a rolling update, old and new versions may exchange messages, share databases, and handle different stages of the same request.

That overlap makes compatibility a system-wide requirement. APIs, message formats, and stored data must work across versions. The rollout also has to preserve capacity and quorum through restarts and partial failures. Rollback can be harder than replacing the binaries because the new version may already have written data the old version cannot read. In effect, the system has to remain correct and available at every intermediate step, including when the rollout stalls halfway through.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A standalone application can often pause, replace its code, and restart. A live distributed system has to keep serving requests while its components change at different times. A single request may pass through both old and new versions, so they must agree on what messages mean and how to read and write shared data.

The hardest part is that an update changes more than code. Once a new version writes data in a format the old version cannot read, rolling back the code can break the service. That makes the transition itself part of the engineering problem. Each stage of the rollout must preserve correctness and availability, even if a node fails and the system stays on mixed versions longer than planned.
